title: CPO's Next Challenge: Turning Optical Performance into Manufacturable Systems
gist: Co-packaged optics (CPO) is moving from lab demos to AI-infrastructure deployment, and the binding constraint is shifting from optical performance to manufacturability: alignment retention, test access, assembly sequence and where defects become visible. Broadcom (Bailly/Tomahawk 5), NVIDIA (Spectrum-X Photonics with detachable fiber) and IBM Research (polymer waveguides) represent different integration-boundary choices that relocate, rather than remove, manufacturing difficulty.

insights.claim: As switch bandwidth rises, the electrical distance between switch silicon and optical transceivers is becoming a key constraint on power efficiency and density, pushing co-packaged optics from lab demonstrations toward commercial AI-infrastructure deployment.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: CPO adoption is driven by AI network power/density limits — a structural tailwind for silicon photonics and advanced packaging suppliers.
insights.locator: The Shift from Optical Performance to Manufacturing Scale

insights.claim: Conventional pluggable optics force high-speed electrical signals across PCBs, which at higher signaling rates adds insertion loss, reflections, equalization requirements and extra power, the problem CPO addresses by moving optical conversion next to the switch ASIC.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Frames the long-run substitution risk for pluggable-transceiver vendors as signaling rates climb.

insights.claim: The next CPO engineering challenge is not better optical performance but preserving that performance through a repeatable, economically viable manufacturing process as the technology moves from demonstrations to sustained production.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Watch yield/assembly capability, not headline Tbps, as the gating factor for CPO ramp timing and supplier winners.
insights.quote: The next engineering challenge is not simply achieving better optical performance. It is preserving that performance through a repeatable and economically viable manufacturing process.

insights.claim: Broadcom's Bailly CPO platform integrates eight silicon-photonics optical engines with a Tomahawk 5 switch ASIC for 51.2 Tbps, maximizing electrical efficiency but moving optical-engine attachment, thermal behavior and fiber coupling closer to the high-value switch silicon.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Broadcom's tight-integration path makes package-level assembly yield the key risk to its CPO economics.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics attaches silicon-photonics engines to the substrate with solder-reflow-compatible processes but uses detachable fiber connectors, so fiber attachment happens later and optical engines can be screened before final integration.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's design keeps a manufacturing boundary that can improve yield and enable automated fiber attachment — relevant to connector and assembly-automation suppliers.

insights.claim: Tight electrical integration and selective manufacturing modularity are not mutually exclusive: architecture determines when a physical interface is formed and which process steps happen before or after it.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Use this lens to compare CPO platforms: ask where each design places its assembly/test boundaries.
insights.quote: tight electrical integration and selective manufacturing modularity are not mutually exclusive

insights.claim: IBM Research has demonstrated CPO module assembly using polymer optical waveguides with different integration sequences and solder-reflow compatibility, but these remain feasibility demonstrations whose production economics still require separate validation.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: IBM's work signals alternative assembly routes but is not yet a commercial volume driver.
insights.locator: IBM Research: Make the Assembly Sequence a Design Variable

insights.claim: Placing an optical engine next to a hot switch ASIC creates a coupled problem: shorter electrical paths cut loss and power, but higher local temperatures, package warpage, material expansion and assembly stress threaten optical alignment and coupling efficiency.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Thermal and mechanical control at the package level becomes a differentiator — favors suppliers of advanced substrates, thermal solutions and alignment equipment.
insights.locator: Consider the placement of an optical engine

insights.claim: An optical engine that is aligned at assembly may not stay aligned: adhesive curing, thermal excursions, substrate warpage and thermal-expansion mismatch can all shift photonic components relative to fiber interfaces.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Retained (post-assembly) optical performance, not initial placement accuracy, is the metric to track for HVM readiness.
insights.quote: A successfully aligned optical engine does not necessarily remain aligned after manufacturing.

insights.claim: Optics-first, optics-last and detachable/modular CPO assembly each relocate manufacturing difficulty rather than eliminating it — exposing optics to later processing, requiring precision attach in a constrained package, or requiring repeatable mating alignment respectively.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: No single CPO assembly flow is a free lunch; expect divergent supplier approaches rather than quick standardization.
insights.quote: Each approach relocates manufacturing difficulty rather than eliminating it.

insights.claim: Passive optical alignment can raise throughput when tolerances are controlled, while active alignment compensates for placement errors at the cost of equipment time and optical feedback; neither guarantees stability after bonding or thermal cycling.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Equipment time for active alignment is a cost and capacity lever in CPO ramps.
insights.locator: Passive alignment may improve manufacturing throughput

insights.claim: Compounding yield matters in CPO: eight independent optical integration steps at 99% acceptance each yield only about 92.3% combined acceptance for the completed assembly (illustrative, ignoring correlation and rework).
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Multi-engine packages carry multiplicative yield risk on expensive switch silicon — a cost headwind early in the ramp.
insights.locator: Suppose an assembly contains eight critical optical

insights.claim: CPO economics hinge on where defects become visible: an optical engine rejected before package integration costs little, while the same defect found after permanent attachment can put the ASIC, substrate, thermal structures and completed testing at risk.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Architectures enabling pre-integration screening or rework (e.g., known-good optical engines) should have better cost curves at volume.
insights.quote: Recoverability becomes an important economic variable.
insights.locator: Now consider when a defect is discovered.

insights.claim: An architecture with slightly more interfaces may be economically preferable if those interfaces enable independent screening or rework, whereas permanent integration wins only once process capability is mature enough to make occasional failures tolerable.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Against the 'maximum integration' consensus — modularity may win early in the CPO ramp.
insights.locator: An architecture with slightly more interfaces

insights.claim: In CPO, design-for-test becomes an architectural requirement because optical probing needs precise alignment, light sources and calibrated receivers, and some optical characteristics are only measurable after EIC/PIC integration or fiber attachment.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Photonic test equipment and test-access design are emerging bottlenecks — watch optical test vendors.
insights.quote: Testability therefore cannot be treated solely as an activity performed after design completion.
insights.locator: Design for Test Becomes an Architectural Requirement

insights.claim: The success of CPO will depend on turning electrical-optical integration into a repeatable, testable, qualified and economically scalable manufacturing process, since the integration boundary is where system performance requirements become manufacturing requirements.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Investors should weight manufacturing-ecosystem readiness (assembly, test, qualification) as heavily as optical specs when timing CPO adoption.
insights.quote: The integration boundary is where system performance requirements become manufacturing requirements.
